Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-boost-transcribe-long-0002", "row_sha256": "809f477fdda626e92270487f913d3b499c6b6fa9b80c5d001efe1eb00ef57165", "mode": "/transcribe", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Remove true hesitation and accidental restarts. Apply explicit corrections to the final stated intent. Preserve meaningful filler-like words and unfinished thoughts. Apply clearly spoken punctuation and list cues. Keep the supplied language.", "input": "i'm dictating the repair notes for the intercom at 46 linden court, apartment building, after the call from residents on tuesday morning. the problem was reported first by joel in 2b, who said the lobby visitor could hear him but he could not hear the visitor. he also said the door release worked on some calls and not on others. the building has three floors and twenty apartments, with the older call panel beside the mailboxes and a separate buzzer for the rear entrance. nobody reported that the rear buzzer was failing. Mara is the building manager, no sorry, she is the night caretaker, and she was the person who let me into the basement utility room. she had received two more reports before i arrived, from residents in 1a and 3c, both describing a one-way conversation rather than a completely dead handset. period

i arrived at 9:10 and checked the panel before taking anything apart. the directory card was faded but readable, and the apartment numbers matched the labels at the indoor handsets. the panel microphone had a loose wire at its terminal, though the insulation was not split. i tightened the terminal screw and gently moved the wire to see whether the sound dropped out. the lobby speaker stayed clear during that check. the door strike clicked when i pressed the release from 2b, but it did not click from the test handset in 1a. that difference made me suspect a problem inside the 1a handset or its branch cable, not the common door lock. i wrote down the time and the apartment used for each test because the first reports had not all described the same symptom. period

Mara showed me a small envelope of earlier service notes. one note from last winter mentioned a wet patch near the conduit above the basement ceiling, but it did not say that water had reached the intercom wiring. the ceiling was dry when i looked, and there was no staining around the junction box. i did see dust packed into the lower edge of the lobby panel, with a few strands of lint over the speaker grille. i brushed that away using a soft paintbrush and did not spray cleaner into the openings. the panel's metal cover was firmly seated after i checked the screws. Mara said the cover had been removed once for painting, and she could not remember whether anyone had opened the wiring compartment at that time. i left the cover in place until i had tested each apartment call. period

start numbered list of checks. number one, call 1a from the lobby and listen at the handset, then test the door release. number two, repeat the call to 2b and compare the visitor's voice at the indoor handset. number three, call 3c and ask the resident to speak from different distances from the microphone. number four, check the rear entrance buzzer separately and do not connect it to the lobby-panel fault unless it shows the same symptom. number five, after the calls, inspect the branch connections in the basement junction box and photograph their positions before loosening anything. end list. i followed that order so i would not mix a handset fault with a panel fault or change the wire layout before recording it. the resident in 1a was home, but 3c was empty until early afternoon, so i completed the first two checks and scheduled the third call for later. period

the 1a handset had a crack near the lower screw and the cord was twisted, but neither issue explained the silent incoming voice by itself. i called from the lobby and heard the bell inside the apartment. the resident lifted the handset and said, quote, i can hear the bell but i still can't hear you, end quote. when i moved the handset cord, the lobby voice came through briefly and then faded again. i removed the handset cover and found one conductor not fully clamped under its terminal. the copper end was intact, and there was no scorch mark or green residue. i reseated the conductor, secured the cover, and called again. both directions of speech were clear through three test calls, and the release button opened the door each time. i told the resident that the handset would need to be watched for another day, because the cracked housing could still loosen under ordinary use. period

at 11:40 i returned to the lobby panel and called 2b. joel answered and said the sound was clearer than it had been that morning. he could hear me without holding his ear close to the handset, and i could hear his replies without static. i asked him to press the release twice, with a pause between presses. the strike clicked both times, and the lobby door opened without sticking. i checked that it latched again after each test. joel said that on monday evening he had needed to press the button three times, but he had not noticed whether the visitor could hear him then. i recorded that as a reported earlier occurrence rather than a fault i had reproduced. the difference matters because the current tests do not establish what happened on monday evening. period

when i opened the basement junction box, the cable labels were handwritten and one had partly peeled away. the pair serving 1a was still identifiable by its number and by tracing it to the riser. i took the requested photograph before touching the connections. the screw terminal for that pair was secure at the junction box, so i did not tighten it just because the handset end had been loose. two unused conductors were capped separately, with no exposed copper touching the box. i left them capped and did not use them as substitutes. the cable sheath was dry, and the route toward the lobby panel showed no visible pinch point where it passed the ceiling bracket. i checked the old conduit note with Mara, and she confirmed that it referred to a maintenance visit after heavy rain, not to a documented leak into the wiring. period

at 1:15 the resident in 3c came home and agreed to a call test. the lobby call rang once, and she answered from beside the kitchen doorway. i could hear her normally there, then asked her to move farther into the apartment. her voice became quieter at the far end of the hall, but it did not break up. she said the handset had worked normally all week and that she had only reported it because the lobby visitor sounded faint during one call on tuesday. i called again while she stood near the handset, and the sound was clear in both directions. the rear entrance buzzer also rang in the apartment, and its separate release worked. that result kept the rear entrance circuit outside the repair i had made to the 1a handset. period

the weather forecast mattered for the final check because rain was expected later. if water appears around the basement conduit or junction box, stop further electrical testing and notify the building contact before opening that area again. Mara agreed to check the ceiling after the rain, since the earlier note gave no evidence of water on the wiring today. i did not mark the old damp report as resolved; i recorded only that the surface and cable route were dry during this visit. before leaving, i confirmed that the panel cover was secure, the directory remained readable, and all twenty apartment buttons were still aligned with their labels. i left the repaired 1a handset in service for observation, with the loose conductor reseated and the cracked housing noted in the work record. the residents in 2b and 3c had clear calls during their tests, and the door strike operated each time i asked it to. period", "output": "I'm dictating the repair notes for the intercom at 46 Linden Court, an apartment building, after the call from residents on Tuesday morning. The problem was reported first by Joel in 2B, who said the lobby visitor could hear him but he could not hear the visitor. He also said the door release worked on some calls and not on others. The building has three floors and twenty apartments, with the older call panel beside the mailboxes and a separate buzzer for the rear entrance. Nobody reported that the rear buzzer was failing. Mara is the night caretaker, and she was the person who let me into the basement utility room. She had received two more reports before I arrived, from residents in 1A and 3C, both describing a one-way conversation rather than a completely dead handset.

I arrived at 9:10 and checked the panel before taking anything apart. The directory card was faded but readable, and the apartment numbers matched the labels at the indoor handsets. The panel microphone had a loose wire at its terminal, though the insulation was not split. I tightened the terminal screw and gently moved the wire to see whether the sound dropped out. The lobby speaker stayed clear during that check. The door strike clicked when I pressed the release from 2B, but it did not click from the test handset in 1A. That difference made me suspect a problem inside the 1A handset or its branch cable, not the common door lock. I wrote down the time and the apartment used for each test because the first reports had not all described the same symptom.

Mara showed me a small envelope of earlier service notes. One note from last winter mentioned a wet patch near the conduit above the basement ceiling, but it did not say that water had reached the intercom wiring. The ceiling was dry when I looked, and there was no staining around the junction box. I did see dust packed into the lower edge of the lobby panel, with a few strands of lint over the speaker grille. I brushed that away using a soft paintbrush and did not spray cleaner into the openings. The panel's metal cover was firmly seated after I checked the screws. Mara said the cover had been removed once for painting, and she could not remember whether anyone had opened the wiring compartment at that time. I left the cover in place until I had tested each apartment call.

1. Call 1A from the lobby and listen at the handset, then test the door release.
2. Repeat the call to 2B and compare the visitor's voice at the indoor handset.
3. Call 3C and ask the resident to speak from different distances from the microphone.
4. Check the rear entrance buzzer separately and do not connect it to the lobby-panel fault unless it shows the same symptom.
5. After the calls, inspect the branch connections in the basement junction box and photograph their positions before loosening anything.

I followed that order so I would not mix a handset fault with a panel fault or change the wire layout before recording it. The resident in 1A was home, but 3C was empty until early afternoon, so I completed the first two checks and scheduled the third call for later.

The 1A handset had a crack near the lower screw and the cord was twisted, but neither issue explained the silent incoming voice by itself. I called from the lobby and heard the bell inside the apartment. The resident lifted the handset and said, “I can hear the bell but I still can't hear you.” When I moved the handset cord, the lobby voice came through briefly and then faded again. I removed the handset cover and found one conductor not fully clamped under its terminal. The copper end was intact, and there was no scorch mark or green residue. I reseated the conductor, secured the cover, and called again. Both directions of speech were clear through three test calls, and the release button opened the door each time. I told the resident that the handset would need to be watched for another day, because the cracked housing could still loosen under ordinary use.

At 11:40 I returned to the lobby panel and called 2B. Joel answered and said the sound was clearer than it had been that morning. He could hear me without holding his ear close to the handset, and I could hear his replies without static. I asked him to press the release twice, with a pause between presses. The strike clicked both times, and the lobby door opened without sticking. I checked that it latched again after each test. Joel said that on Monday evening he had needed to press the button three times, but he had not noticed whether the visitor could hear him then. I recorded that as a reported earlier occurrence rather than a fault I had reproduced. The difference matters because the current tests do not establish what happened on Monday evening.

When I opened the basement junction box, the cable labels were handwritten and one had partly peeled away. The pair serving 1A was still identifiable by its number and by tracing it to the riser. I took the requested photograph before touching the connections. The screw terminal for that pair was secure at the junction box, so I did not tighten it just because the handset end had been loose. Two unused conductors were capped separately, with no exposed copper touching the box. I left them capped and did not use them as substitutes. The cable sheath was dry, and the route toward the lobby panel showed no visible pinch point where it passed the ceiling bracket. I checked the old conduit note with Mara, and she confirmed that it referred to a maintenance visit after heavy rain, not to a documented leak into the wiring.

At 1:15 the resident in 3C came home and agreed to a call test. The lobby call rang once, and she answered from beside the kitchen doorway. I could hear her normally there, then asked her to move farther into the apartment. Her voice became quieter at the far end of the hall, but it did not break up. She said the handset had worked normally all week and that she had only reported it because the lobby visitor sounded faint during one call on Tuesday. I called again while she stood near the handset, and the sound was clear in both directions. The rear entrance buzzer also rang in the apartment, and its separate release worked. That result kept the rear entrance circuit outside the repair I had made to the 1A handset.

The weather forecast mattered for the final check because rain was expected later. If water appears around the basement conduit or junction box, stop further electrical testing and notify the building contact before opening that area again. Mara agreed to check the ceiling after the rain, since the earlier note gave no evidence of water on the wiring today. I did not mark the old damp report as resolved; I recorded only that the surface and cable route were dry during this visit. Before leaving, I confirmed that the panel cover was secure, the directory remained readable, and all twenty apartment buttons were still aligned with their labels. I left the repaired 1A handset in service for observation, with the loose conductor reseated and the cracked housing noted in the work record. The residents in 2B and 3C had clear calls during their tests, and the door strike operated each time I asked it to."}]
